1:
Robertson counts six separate marks of time here and reads the pile-up as deliberate: the prophetic voice had been silent for centuries, and its return was worth dating. Gregory finds a reason in the pairing. John preached a Redeemer for some among the Jews and many among the Gentiles, so the date is taken from a Gentile sovereign and the princes of Judea together; one man is named over the Roman state because all nations were to be gathered into one, and priests as well as rulers because the One preached was at once King and Priest. Origen sets the method against the older prophets, whose visions were dated by the kings of Judah alone because spoken to Jews alone, where a Gospel for the whole world is dated by the man who seemed lord of it. Gregory adds that the Jewish realm is split among petty governors because a kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation. Henry hears the same note: the lawgiver had departed from between Judah's feet, and a people dating its public acts by a foreign emperor is one for whom Shiloh must come.

The arithmetic divides. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley reckon the fifteenth year from the two years of joint rule, making it the thirteenth of the sole reign. Calvin works instead from Josephus, allowing Valerius Gratus his eleven years and placing the preaching in Pilate's second year; Bede has Pilate sent out in the twelfth year of Tiberius to stay almost ten. Lysanias divides them further. Bede makes him a son of Herod the Great alongside Herod and Philip; Calvin rejects the identification with the son of Ptolemy Mennaeus, long since killed by Cleopatra, and proposes a grandson of the same name; Robertson meets the objection from Josephus with an inscription found at Abilene naming Lysanias the tetrarch at just this period, and says the evangelist is vindicated again by the rocks. Barnes and Clarke turn the apparatus into an argument: an impostor does not scatter names, dates and provinces any contemporary could check.

Two high priests at once is harder. Gill will not have it, citing the rule that they do not appoint two high priests at one time, and rejecting alternating years as unattested. Lightfoot answers with the sagan, standing to the high priest as the second man stands to the king, and refuses to identify him with the substitute held ready against defilement on the day of expiation. Clarke and Wesley make Annas the high priest and Caiaphas his deputy; Barnes turns it around, giving the office to Caiaphas and treating Annas as the deposed predecessor who still held civil power, named first as elder and father-in-law. Calvin denies either shared the title, showing from the same historian how freely the Roman governor gave and withdrew it. Bede notes three others held it between.

On the call itself there is no quarrel. Ambrose observes that the third evangelist proves John a prophet in five words and adds nothing, where the others reach for the raiment and the girdle and the food; enough, since those filled with the Word need no judgment of their own. The wilderness is the Church, the barren woman with more children than the married. Chrysostom presses that the word was a command, for he came not of himself, and Calvin draws the ministerial rule, that having the word is not a calling to preach it. Theophylact explains the long hiding: had John grown up in his kinsman's company, the witness could have been put down to acquaintance, and so he could say he knew him not. Gregory of Nyssa sees him withdrawn from the senses and their forced notions, in the spirit and power of Elias. Henry adds the quiet irony that a priest's son entering his thirtieth year should have gone onto the temple roll, and is enrolled here instead.
3:
Ambrose marks the order: the Word came first and the voice followed, because the Word works inward before the office of the voice begins. Origen reads the ground, taking Jordan to mean descending and finding there the river of healing water that comes down from God, so that the circuit John walks brings a penitent quickly to the stream. Gill places him out of the wilderness in the parts bordering the river, at Bethabara and at Aenon near Salim, and observes that he made no tour of the region; the region came to him. Robertson fills in the map, the valley called El Ghor reaching north as far as Succoth, usually the western bank and sometimes the eastern, his baptizing keeping him near the water.

What a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins can mean, with the sacrifice not yet offered, is pressed hard. Gregory grants that John both preached and administered it, and denies flatly that it could remit. Chrysostom asks how remission could be given before the Spirit had descended, and answers that the phrase states the aim rather than the effect: the Jews did not know the weight of their sins, and John came to convince them of it, that they might seek a Redeemer and be ready to receive pardon. Calvin turns the words into a rule for sacraments, that a sign without the Word is a dumb ceremony and unmeaning pomp, and concludes that since the meaning, power and nature are one, it is wrong to call John's baptism a different thing from ours. Robertson adds that the word for remission is commoner in this evangelist than in all other writers of the New Testament together, and that medical writers use it of a disease relaxing.

On the prophecy the witnesses supply one custom from opposite ends of the world. Clarke reports the Hindoo kings who sent men ahead to have the inhabitants clear the roads, a necessity where there are no public ways; Robertson recalls the people of Brusa turned out to clear rocks and fill hollows before the Sultan's visit. Cyril of Alexandria takes the herald's office as the lamp before the true light and the morning star before the sun, a voice and not a Word, and reads preparing the way as withdrawing the heart from the shadow of the law and ceasing from the types. He grounds it in the soul: created beautiful and straight, so that vice is its perversion, and if we continue as we were made we shall be virtuous. Cyril of Jerusalem hears the cry as still sounding, joined to the prophet's call to those who thirst.

The levelled ground is read four ways. Origen makes the mountains and hills the hostile powers thrown down at Christ's coming, and Basil refines it: as hills and mountains differ only in height, those powers agree in purpose and differ in the enormity of their offences. Gregory reads an exchange, the Gentiles filled with the grace the Jews forfeited, the proud held off from the gift the humble receive. Chrysostom makes it the hard road of the law turned into the easy road of faith. Gregory of Nyssa takes it as a measure, virtue failing neither by defect nor excess. Gill and Lightfoot both record what the rabbis did with the passage, the cloud that levelled hills and raised valleys and killed the serpents, and the restriction of the promise to bringing back the captivity. Against that narrowing Calvin argues that the return from exile cannot have fulfilled it, since this salvation was to strike every eye, and notes that flesh here means simply men, with no charge of corruption. Wesley reads the salvation of God as the Saviour. Gregory alone refuses the present reference, stretching the sight of all flesh to the day of judgment, when elect and reprobate see him alike.
7:
Who is called a brood of vipers is disputed. Ellicott judges the first Gospel more accurate in aiming the words at the Pharisees and Sadducees, and Gill and Calvin read them so, Calvin adding that the rebuke was public for the bystanders' sake, that others also might fear. Robertson resists the harmonising: the noun is plural and the verb an imperfect, so this evangelist reports what John used to say to crowd after crowd, and adds that every image he reaches for, vipers and axe and chaff, comes off the wilderness floor. Origen takes it from the participle, that the warning falls on those still going out toward the water, since had they truly come forth he would not have called them vipers at all.

The name itself is worked over. Chrysostom observes that the man of the desert, with all Palestine standing round him in admiration, did not bend under that respect but reproved them, and notes how freely Scripture assigns beasts to passions, dogs for impudence, asps for guile. He supplies the natural history behind the insult: the female viper kills the male, and the young kill the mother as they burst out, so the breed are parricides, as were those who killed their teachers. Gregory makes them poisonous sons of poisonous parents by imitation, and reads the wrath to come as final punishment awarded. Against this Ambrose allows the crowd more credit, finding a prudence that perceives what is coming and seeks help, even while they do not let go of what harms them. Chrysostom raises the objection squarely, that men beginning to turn deserve comfort, not rebuke, and answers that John judged not by what showed but by hearts disclosed to him, striking at their boasting without blaming the patriarchs. Cyril of Alexandria goes further: the Baptist foresaw the slanders to be flung at Christ, and called even the repentant wicked.

On the fruits they agree. Chrysostom insists that leaving off sin is not enough, since healing wants a salve and not merely the drawing of the arrow, and notes the plural, which signifies abundance. Gregory presses the word worthy into a rule of proportion: one who has fallen must cut himself off from what is lawful in the measure of the unlawful he committed, equal fruit not serving unequal guilt. Chrysostom denies Abraham's line is disowned, only that descent avails nothing where the kinship of virtue is missing; Cyril asks what inherited nobility profits a man fallen away from his ancestors' virtues; Basil answers with the horse, whose sire's speed does not make him swift, a man being praised by his own present worth. Gregory of Nyssa hears in the stones the calling of the Gentiles. Ambrose prefers the mystery to the miracle: those who bowed to stones were stones themselves, and faith is to be poured into such hearts. Lightfoot, without pressing the play on the two Hebrew words, hears plain scorn: they were such children of Abraham as God could match out of gravel.

The axe divides them again. Origen, noting how many ages have passed, refers it to Israel, whose cutting off was near, and Gill names the Romans already in the land as the axe in God's hand, laid to the root of covenant, polity and boast. Cyril holds the tool laid near the root rather than fixed to it, the branches cut but the tree standing, a remnant to be saved. Gregory shifts the figure, making the tree the human race and the axe the Redeemer, held by human hand yet striking with divine power, set at the root because whole households, not merely children, are removed. Cyril of Jerusalem turns it on the hearer, bidding him shed the old skin as a serpent does, and warning the man who came only to spy out the grace that the Judge is inexorable.
10:
Gregory reads the question as the mark of troubled hearers, and Origen notes three classes coming forward, the crowd, the collectors and the men under arms. Theophylact finds the replies shaped to each: those in no evil trade are told to do good, the other two what to stop. Robertson sees the same tailoring, that John lays his finger on the weakness of whoever stands in front of him, and notes the imperfect, a question put again and again. Ellicott adds that these exchanges belong to this Gospel alone and show the Baptist doing more than preach repentance: confession drew guidance after it, and a physician of souls would relish such therapy. Calvin makes the reply a test, since the world prefers to discharge its debt to God by ceremony, and the second Table is the surer mark, with less room for self-deception.

How far the sharing goes divides them. Gregory presses that the garment named is the more necessary one, so what is asked is not surplus but what a man needs. Basil goes further, that whatever exceeds daily support is owed to the man who has nothing, and he loves his neighbour less than himself who withholds necessities; a coat divided clothes nobody. Ambrose holds the line differently: mercy is the fullness of the virtues and owed in common rather than case by case, yet a proportion is kept, and no man must strip himself bare. Lightfoot explains the phrasing, since some counted it religion to wear a single garment. Theophylact reports the reading that makes the coats letter and spirit, the man holding both owing the ignorant at least the letter. Cyril of Jerusalem grounds the demand in the preacher, who practised what he taught, and asks whether a man who will not part with bread can expect greater gifts.

With the collectors they defend the office and condemn the practice. Chrysostom marvels that the rich should seek salvation from a man who owns nothing, and explains the modest counsel as accommodation, John withholding a wisdom they could not bear. Barnes and Clarke insist the work is honourable, since a state must be supported and someone must gather what is due, so only the surcharge is sin; Clarke turns this on the assessors of his own day. Ellicott traces the temptation to the Roman farming of taxes, and Robertson the odium of a Jew collecting for Rome, where the verb for exacting came to mean working the public like blood-suckers. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic side, collectors ruled unfit to give evidence, and one remembered for thirteen honest years who waved the teachers out of sight lest the governor count them and raise the tax.

Who the soldiers were is disputed. Gill takes them for Jews in the pay of Herod or Philip, Barnes will not decide, and Ellicott rejects a Roman identification outright, reading the participle as men on the march and placing them with the troops of Antipas moving down the valley against Aretas, whose daughter he had put away. On the two orders there is agreement without certainty. Clarke matches the first to the Roman offence of extortion, Robertson to a shaking that terrifies money loose. The second word is the crux: Barnes gives the Athenian fig-informer as its origin, while Ellicott and Robertson both report that no instance of that usage survives. Lightfoot describes the trade instead, the whispered secret that makes the hearer liable too. Ambrose reads the word on wages as the reason pay exists, lest armed men turn robbers to supply themselves. Augustine draws the largest conclusion: John could have said lay down your arms, and did not, because men under arms are ministers of law and defenders of public safety rather than killers, and what is blamed in war is not that mortal men die but the lust of power and the cruelty of revenge.
15:
The suspense had reasons. Gill and Henry name them: the seventy weeks running out, the sceptre gone from Judah with no king but Caesar, and Henry adds that the lawgiver too had gone, Herod having lately destroyed the council. Barnes renders the mood as doubt, not settled opinion, and Robertson sharpens the puzzle: John worked no miracle and stood outside David's line, yet moved men so far that they suspected him, a suspicion the council would later put to him formally. Ellicott notes that this musing is preserved here alone, matches the fourth Gospel, and repairs the abruptness with which the mightier one is introduced elsewhere. Clarke credits the reach of the reformation, a preacher who told crowd, collector and soldier each his duty.

The fathers are more anxious about the affection than the mistake. Origen grants that John deserved more deference than other men, having lived as none did, then turns it to a warning: love without measure is dangerous, and where it passes what the object deserves both lover and loved are in fault. Ambrose adds an argument from absurdity, that men willing to find the Christ in one born of a woman would not believe him born of a virgin, the virgin birth being the very mark of the coming. Bede asks how he could answer a thought held in secret, and answers from the priests and Levites who came and asked him outright. Ambrose credits the reading of hearts to grace, not native power, and finds the disclaimer made by work and not only word: water washes the body while the Spirit cleanses the soul, so the baptism of repentance, man's work, stands apart from the baptism of grace, which is God's gift. He denies that mightier is a comparison at all, none being possible between the Son of God and a man.

Augustine meets the discrepancy between bearing the shoes and loosing the latchet by supposing John said each at different times, or both, and adds that since either means only his own lowness and his Master's height, both evangelists kept the sense. Gregory reaches for the custom by which a kinsman who would not take the widow he owed had his shoe loosed, so John refuses the bridegroom's name, and adds that shoes being cut from dead beasts, the Lord in flesh went shod in the carcass of our corruption.

What the fire is divides them further. Chrysostom keeps it gracious, noting that John says baptize and not give, which signifies abundance, and reads fire as the fervour of grace and the consuming of sins. Bede allows that the Spirit himself may be meant, kindling with love and enlightening with wisdom, and coming on the apostles in that appearance; but he reports others who divide the two, the Spirit now and fire hereafter for lighter sins. Origen states that view plainly, the Lord standing in the fiery stream with the flaming sword to bathe whoever still needs purifying before paradise, and refusing it to any lacking the seal of earlier baptisms. Against such comfort Gregory of Nyssa warns that the punishments bear no proportion to what the senses know, and that the word unquenched is there to stop us imagining an ordinary fire; Gregory presses the point physically, our fire dying without fuel while that one, once made, needs none. Basil turns the verse elsewhere: a baptism invoking the Spirit alone is no baptism, the tradition admitting neither addition nor subtraction. On the threshing-floor a Greek expositor finds the speed of judgment, separation in an instant, not by trial; Cyril reads the floor as Christ's own and the chaff as the light and empty, carried off by any wind of sin; Bede makes it the present Church, the winnowing going on case by case, the open offender put out by the priesthood, the secret one left to the judgment after death.
18:
The summary line draws attention to what is missing. Origen takes it as an admission that much was left unwritten, the same reticence the fourth Gospel shows about Christ's own words, and holds that some of what John said was too great to be committed to writing. Theophylact makes a point of the verb, that an exhortation which tells good things is properly called gospel, so that the forerunner was already an evangelist. Ellicott observes that this is the one record insisting on the breadth of that teaching, and guesses that whatever source supplied the answers to crowd, collector and soldier supplied more of the same, what all three keep in common being the text and burden of it. Robertson reads the phrase as many and varied things, and judges what survives a bare sample that still yields a definite and powerful conception of the preaching. Gill fills the gap from elsewhere, taking the unrecorded matter to concern the person of the Messiah, the nature of his kingdom and faith in him.

Origen then turns to the courage. None born of women was greater, and by his deeds he had been raised so high that men mistook him for the Christ; but the greater marvel is that he neither feared Herod nor shrank from death. Eusebius supplies the grounds of the quarrel: the tetrarch, so titled to distinguish him from the king in whose reign Christ was born, had a wife already, the Arabian king's daughter, and had taken his brother's wife although she had borne that brother children, the old permission reaching only to a brother who died childless. He adds that Herod at first listened closely, knowing the words weighty and full of consolation, until the woman's will made him despise them.

Robertson works the vocabulary. The verb for reproving runs from treating with contempt in the old poets to convicting and exposing, and he cites the historian on how repulsive the marriage was to Jewish feeling; the adjective for the evil deeds gives the active side of evil, mischief worked rather than mere defect, the word behind the mischief-working eye and behind the evil one; and the last verb is a plain summary aorist, not a pluperfect. On the word for adding he is careful in the other direction: the old physicians used it of laying wet sponges on the head and of dosing with acorns, and he states flatly that there is no evidence of a medical turn here. The verb for shutting up, he notes, means literally to shut down, perhaps on a dungeon door.

Whether this was the worst of Herod's acts is disputed. Barnes denies it, taking the phrase to mean only that this was one more deed of the same character, and explains its early position as a way of finishing John's account before the narrative moves on. Wesley gives the same reason, that the history of the forerunner is concluded here so that the Lord's may run on without interruption. Gill reads the words the other way, as marking a sin more flagitious than the others and worse in its outcome. Bede takes the placing chronologically, noting that the fourth Gospel puts the arrest after miracles had been done and the Lord's baptizing was talked of, and accounting for the difference by a redoubled malice in Herod, who watched the crowds flocking, the soldiers believing and the collectors repenting, and moved early. Calvin names the prison and weighs the sources: the historian puts John in the fortress of Machaerus and ascribes the arrest to fear of insurrection, and makes Herodias the wife of another Herod rather than of Philip; but since his memory fails here, and he sets Philip's death in the wrong place, Calvin holds the certain account to be the evangelists' and abides by their testimony.
21:
Ambrose notices that this account only summarises what others told at length, and states the reason: the Lord went into the water not to be cleansed but to cleanse it, so that waters purified by the flesh of one who knew no sin might afterwards carry the power of baptism. Gregory Nazianzen puts it shorter, that he came to bury the old Adam in the water. Chrysostom grades three washings: the older rites reached the flesh and not the conscience, John's turned men from sin to virtue, and ours goes further, his conveying neither the Spirit nor remission by grace.

Henry makes much of the order, that Christ was baptized last, in the rear of the common people, humbling himself as less than the least, and prayed without confessing, having nothing to confess. Robertson finds the text will not carry it: the infinitive has no time in it, and the sentence says only that the baptism happened in connection with the baptizing of the people at large, not after it. The praying is peculiar to this Gospel, but the participle gives only that heaven opened while Jesus prayed, not because he prayed. Barnes places the scene after the administration, not during it.

On the descent the concern is that nothing be conceded to adoptionism. Chrysostom insists the Son did not receive what he lacked, sending the Spirit from above as God and receiving him below as man, the movement running from his deity to his humanity, and he received for us as head of the race. Augustine meets the difficulty of a gift at thirty by arguing that one whose conception was not carnal came to the water no more without the Spirit than without innocence, and that the scene prefigures the Church, where the baptized receive him.

Why a dove is answered variously. Ambrose takes innocence and peace, recalling the bird that carried the olive to the ark that outlived the flood. Cyprian argues from the creature, which has no gall, no fierce bite, no tearing claws, keeps one home and flies wing to wing, a law of unanimity. Chrysostom contrasts Pentecost, gentleness while offences are pardoned and fire when trial comes. What was seen, and by whom, is less settled. Barnes takes a real appearance witnessed by the people, the Spirit's visible forms being always emblematic. Gill restricts the sight to the baptizer, for whom it was a signal. Robertson agrees the Baptist saw it and warns against the old error that made this the beginning of the Incarnation. Ellicott leaves it open, allowing that the words may describe a descent after the manner of a dove, hovering then settling, in some undefined bodily form. Cyril of Jerusalem settles the purpose rather than the appearance: the sight was given not that Jesus might see the Spirit, whom he knew already, but for John's sake. Lightfoot adds the rabbinic curiosity of a golden dove atop Solomon's sceptre.

The voice is handled as doctrine. Ambrose observes that the Spirit was seen and the Father only heard, and that taking no body he proved his presence in the Son by speaking. Athanasius presses the article: sons by grace are one thing, Isaac son of Abraham another, and only the second sense will do, or the Only-begotten differs in nothing from us. God cannot be divided, he adds, and so begets without suffering; and beloved follows from the Son's singleness, a father of many having his affection divided. Bede reads the good pleasure as a commission, what the Father means to do through him. Gregory takes it by contrast with repentance: a man who amends has displeased himself, and the Father who spoke of repenting that he made man found nothing in Christ to repent of. Augustine harmonises the two forms by noting that nothing was revealed to Christ, who knew it: the announcement was for the bystanders.
23:
Whether thirty is a significant number divides the witnesses. Gill, Clarke and Wesley take it as the age the law required of those who served in the sanctuary, Wesley adding that the ministry, not the birthday, is being dated. Ellicott corrects the detail: the Levites entered full service then, after a probation begun at twenty-five or later at twenty, while no age was fixed for priest or prophet, so the most one may infer is that thirty was reckoned the completeness of manhood, for which the Lord waited in patient humility. Barnes denies the inference outright, since Jesus was not under the Levitical law of the priesthood and teachers commonly began earlier. Robertson is blunter: the familiar rendering is impossible, the participle wanting the words to teach supplied, and Tyndale had it right that he was about thirty when he began. He refuses to fix the figure, since prophets begin when the word of God comes to them, and the age may be out by a year either way. Calvin ties the delay to the office, not the calendar, baptism being an appendage of the Gospel, beginning when the preaching did.

Origen reads the direction of the list as the point. It climbs rather than descends, from Christ to God, and he ties the word began to the baptism: having undergone the mystery of the second birth he is said to begin, that you might undo your first and be born in the second. Gregory Nazianzen draws three lessons from who was baptized, by whom and when: the washed must not return to their vomit; no man should speak against a steward of the mysteries he happens to outrank; and no one trusting in his youth should think any age fit for teaching. Chrysostom explains the reach of the two lists by their readers, one written for Jews content to have Christ from Abraham and David, the other for all men and so carried back to Adam. Henry makes the same contrast, adding the older promise of the Seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent.

The qualification as was supposed is handled with care. Clarke notes that the same phrase serves the old historian for a man only reputed to be another's son, and that the ascending list uses an indeterminate form covering sons real or putative, where the descending one means natural generation. Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic parable in which an orphan asked her father's name can name only the man who raised her, with the maxim that he who educates a child is called father, not he who begets; Joseph had owned him from birth, redeemed him as firstborn and brought him up.

On the two lists the proposals are old and various. Augustine offers three ways of reconciling them: one names the father who begot Joseph and the other a maternal grandfather or remoter ancestor; or one names the natural and the other the adopting father; or the levirate is at work, a kinsman raising up seed credited to the dead man. Ambrose gives the levirate version as a story, Matthas of Solomon's line leaving a widow whom Melchi took, Heli coming of her. Wesley takes Heli for the father of Mary and the list for hers, the Jews marrying within their families, so her descent is implied in the other. Ellicott lays out the same options and inclines to the last, treating the reference to Joseph as a parenthesis and the list as the mother's, which would make the Lord of David's seed on both sides, through Nathan by her and Solomon by his reputed father; he suspects the material reached this evangelist through the women round the mother of Jesus. Henry declines to arbitrate, holding that learned men have removed the difficulties, that salvation does not hang on solving them, and that the Gospels' authority is not weakened by them.
24:
This stretch of names is where the textual difficulties gather, and the witnesses treat them soberly. Gill reports at the head of it that Grotius wished two of the names struck out, holding them absent from the ancient exemplars and citing a long row of early authorities in support; Gill declines to follow him, on the ground that the Latin version and all the Oriental versions alike keep them. The dispute is left standing rather than settled.

For several of the names Gill supplies identifications and terms of office drawn from a list of Jewish rulers, giving one a second name and ten years of government, another a second name and nine, and reading a third as the John who was son of Rhesa and governed fifty-three. Whatever the value of the source, the effect is to treat the list as a register of real men in public life rather than a chain of bare names. Gill also groups the long run from Addi down to Mattatha as men who lived before the captivity and belonged to the house of David through the line of Nathan, which is the thread that holds this section of the descent together.

Two problems cluster at Zorobabel. Lightfoot notes first that the father named for him in the older register is missing here, and observes that the omission matches the way the returning leader is named elsewhere in the books written after the exile, while frankly admitting that why he should be dropped in either place is not easy to guess. His second observation is more inventive: Zorobabel and his sons were carried from Babylon into Judea, and men who change their dwelling may change their names, the more so since it was hardly safe to be commonly known in Babylon by a name that meant the winnowing of Babel.

Ellicott approaches the same knot from the royal side. He takes the line descended from Solomon to have expired in Jeconiah, whose childlessness the older prophet's language at least suggests, so that Salathiel, son of Neri and representative of Nathan's line, stepped into the place of inheritance; and he notes the complication in the older register, where the leader of the return is son of Salathiel's brother rather than of Salathiel himself. He finds it significant that in a prophecy of the same period the house of Nathan appears for the first time in the history with a pre-eminence of its own, which is what his reconstruction would require.
30:
From Jesse back to Abraham the difficulties fall away, and Gill says so plainly. Running the names off in order, Obed and Boaz and Salmon, Naasson and Aminadab and Aram, Esrom and Phares, then Judah and Jacob and Isaac and Abraham, he finds that this stretch agrees perfectly with the descent given by the other evangelist and with the accounts in the older books. It is the one long run of the chapter where the two lists and the earlier registers say the same thing, and no reconciliation is called for.

The only textual note Gill enters here is a small one, that the Arabic version inserts a further name, Joram, into the sequence, and that the insertion is to be rejected. Barnes adds nothing but his references, and they are the useful ones: the point at which Nathan is named among the sons born to David, and the prophecy that sets the house of Nathan apart among the families that mourn, together with the older record of the line that runs down to Jesse.
34:
One name here has drawn more argument than the rest. Gill takes the hardest line: the Cainan set between Arphaxad and Salah is absent from the Hebrew, the Samaritan, the Targum, the historian, the place where the older register repeats the descent, and the oldest Greek copy of this Gospel. He grants the name stands in present copies of the Greek version but denies it was ever there, reversing the usual account: a careless early copyist of this Gospel put it in, and it was afterwards carried back into the Greek version to give it authority. The error must be early, reaching many Greek copies, the Latin and every Oriental version; he holds nonetheless that it belongs in no text and no version, no such person having existed.

Bede states the opposite relation without treating it as a fault. Noting that neither the first book nor the Chronicles knows the name, and that Arphaxad there begets Salah with nobody between, he concludes that the evangelist took the generation from the Greek version, and quotes its ages. Lightfoot refuses to reopen a controversy already sufficiently bandied, agrees the Greek version was followed, then turns to a second-hand error: an early writer who follows that version in adding a hundred years to Arphaxad, yet omits Cainan, had the name inserted by a translator who found it nowhere in the original. Clarke reports the expedient of treating Cainan as a surname and reading the two as one, admitting that if this does not untie the knot it cuts it. Ellicott offers the alternative squarely: either the Greek version rests on a Hebrew text older than ours, or, its copies being all made for Christian use, the name was inserted there to match the older list to this one. He notes it is missing from the Latin, Syriac and Samaritan Pentateuchs and from one of the best manuscripts here, then declines to go further with a question he calls infinitesimally small.

The fathers read the closing names for themselves. Ambrose will not have Noah passed over, since one born the builder of his Church sent ahead the man who founded a church in the figure of an ark. He makes something of the reckoning that carries Methuselah's years past the flood, so that in his ancestors as in himself the life that knows no ageing might seem untouched; and he presses Enoch hardest, arguing that a forebear was taken up without dying, which shows Christ need not have died and chose a death to profit us. He keeps the difference in view: Enoch was removed lest wickedness alter his heart, while the Lord, whom wickedness could not alter, returned by his own greatness to the place he came from. Bede counts the steps and finds Enoch at the seventy-seventh in the climb from the baptized Son to God the Father.

On the last words the concern is what sonship means of Adam. Ellicott holds that the form of the list requires them to be read of him, humanity as an immediate creative act being God's offspring, and that the angel's words imply the Lord's human nature had the same title by a like act, so what is true of the second Adam is partly true of the first. He thinks the reach back to Adam suits a Gospel written for the brotherhood of mankind, making Christ the second Adam where the other makes him heir of Abraham; and he defends such records, since the historian transcribed his own pedigree from public registers, priestly births were registered across Babylon and Alexandria with copies sent to Jerusalem, and David's house was not likely to be less careful than Aaron's. Wesley puts the doctrine in a line: Adam received immediately from God whatever his sons receive from human parents, sin and misery excepted. Gill notes only that the Greek version spells another name differently.
